newsitem.title: USA: Storms batter north Texas, airlines cancel flights.
newsitem.headline: Storms batter north Texas, airlines cancel flights.

text.p: Powerful storms ripped through north Texas on Monday, wrecking dozens of apartments, toppling trees and downing power lines and forcing the cancellation of many flights in and out of Dallas.

About 140 people were left homeless when a severe thunderstorm with gusting winds of about 80 mph (120 kph) tore into a low-rent apartment complex in south Dallas. It ripped roofs from dozens of apartments, throwing them and air conditioning units onto parked cars and into the streets.

Seven people including two babies were hurt by flying debris and one man broke his leg, but no serious injuries were reported. Some local residents said a tornado briefly emerged from the storm and battered the neighborhood, forcing residents and construction workers to dive for cover.

American Airlines said it had to cancel 175 flights, or about 25 percent of its daily schedule, in and out of Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport. All of its other flights were running three or four hours behind schedule on Monday, airline spokesman John Hotard said.
Other airlines operating out of Dallas-Fort Worth were also forced to cancel flights as delays mounted, but the situation was better at Dallas' smaller Love Field airport.

The storms dumped up to 4 inches (10 cm) of rain in some areas and flash floods caused traffic chaos in Dallas, Fort Worth and neighboring towns. Further damage to vehicles and homes was caused by pounding, baseball-sized hail across the so-called metroplex.
"I was driving a pretty good sized truck but that wind just blew it straight sideways," said Chuck Dingler.

Meteorological experts said several waves of storms were sweeping through north Texas and would move into southern Arkansas later on Monday. They said a cold front moving down from Canada and a strong upper-level system in New Mexico was to blame for the bad weather causing heavy storms in the front's warm sector and about 2 inches (5 cm) of snow to fall on much of the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles.
Electric company officials said about 23,000 homes in and around Dallas suffered power cuts and repair crews were out restoring lines.
Six private planes were badly damaged at the small Spinks Airport near Fort Worth when swirling winds tore the hangar apart.
